Fighting the fortress only bleeds the company against ground it was never meant to take, and counts as a failure even though it looks like initiative.

complications.name: The Fortress Reacts
complications.text: Once {NPC:opfor-commander} understands the waystation is the target, he will try to save it — detaching a relief column from the fortress's mobile reserve to drive back and break the seizure. The race is whether the company takes and consolidates the waystation before that column arrives, because a relief reaching an un-secured depot turns the quick cut into a stand-up fight in the fortress's rear.
complications.mechanicalEffect: A relief column sorties from the fortress on a clock once the seizure is recognized. Taking and consolidating the waystation before it arrives makes the cut clean; a relief reaching a contested depot forces the company to fight it (the bonus) or lose the hold.

complications.name: The Open Transit Ground
complications.text: The waystation sits on open ground — the transit country the fortress protects — which is fast going both ways. It lets the company reach the depot quickly and lets the fortress's relief reach it quickly too, and offers little cover for the hold once the depot is taken. Speed is the company's weapon and the defender's as well.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The approach and the relief both move fast over open terrain with little cover; the company's hold of the waystation must reckon with exposed ground and the speed at which the relief can close, favoring a fast seizure and prepared blocking positions over a leisurely consolidation.

complications.name: The Stiffened Depot
complications.text: If the defender guessed the plan, the lightly held depot is not so lightly held. The waystation may have been reinforced since the last look — a stronger garrison, dug-in positions added when {NPC:opfor-commander} began to worry about his rear — turning the quick seizure into a real fight against the clock of the fortress's relief.
complications.mechanicalEffect: On a roll at the waystation, the garrison is reinforced beyond the report, lengthening the seizure and squeezing the window before the fortress's relief column arrives, raising the risk of being caught between the depot's garrison and the relief.

decisionPoints.name: Taking the Connector
decisionPoints.context: A lightly held depot behind a strong fortress, and a relief column that starts the moment the move is read. You can race straight for the waystation and seize it before the fortress reacts, cut the connecting routes first to isolate it slowly, or set a blocking force on the relief road to buy the seizure time. Each answer trades speed, the clean cut, and your exposed flank differently.

options.title: Race for the Waystation
advantages: The fastest seizure — takes the depot before the fortress can detach a relief at all
A waystation taken and consolidated early makes the cut clean and the fortress's sortie pointless
disadvantages: A headlong race may arrive disorganized against a depot stiffer than reported
Committing everything forward leaves nothing watching the relief road if the seizure runs long
options.consequence: You bet on speed to make the whole operation moot for the defender; seize the depot fast and the fortress is stranded before it can act, but a slow seizure leaves you with the relief arriving and no one watching the road.

costs.resource: the company committed forward in a race, with nothing held to watch the relief road
costs.risk: A stiffened depot slows the seizure and the relief arrives on an unguarded road — caught between garrison and column

options.title: Cut the Connecting Routes First
advantages: Severing the depot's links isolates it before assaulting, ensuring the fortress is cut even if the seizure runs long
Cutting the routes also slows or blocks the fortress's relief on the same roads
disadvantages: Working the routes first spends time the fortress uses to react, and telegraphs the move
Dividing effort onto the routes leaves less weight for the seizure itself
options.consequence: You guarantee the cut by isolating the depot before taking it, at the cost of speed and surprise; the fortress is stranded regardless, but the slower tempo gives the defender his best chance to interfere.

costs.resource: time and an element spent cutting the connecting routes before the seizure
costs.risk: The slower, telegraphed approach lets the fortress stiffen the depot and ready its relief before the seizure even begins

options.title: Block the Relief Road
advantages: A blocking force on the relief road buys the seizure the time it needs by holding off the fortress's column
A blocked or ambushed relief can be destroyed (the bonus), weakening the fortress further
disadvantages: Splitting off a blocking force leaves fewer guns for the waystation seizure itself
The blocking force on open ground faces the fortress's mobile reserve with its back to the depot it is protecting
options.consequence: You protect the seizure by meeting the relief head-on with part of your weight, trading a divided force for a secured window; done right the relief is broken and the cut is clean, done wrong both halves are too light.

costs.resource: a blocking element committed to the relief road, away from the seizure
costs.risk: The fortress's reserve overpowers the blockers on open ground — the relief breaks through to the depot mid-seizure

entries.event: The company reaches the waystation's approaches; the depot garrison stands to and the sector recognizes a force in the fortress's rear.
{NPC:opfor-commander} reads the target as the waystation and orders a relief column detached from the fortress's mobile reserve.
The seizure of the depot should be well underway; the relief column starts back from the fortress.
The relief column nears the waystation's approaches; the depot must be taken and consolidated, or held against both garrison and relief.
The cut is permanent and the fortress stranded, or the relief has broken through and the connector stays open.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The waystation must be seized and consolidated by T+22:00, before the fortress's relief column can reopen it. A depot still contested when the relief arrives turns the clean bypass into a stand-up fight in the enemy's rear, and a fortress left connected is a strongpoint the campaign must still storm the hard way.

opforSketch.composition: A light depot garrison plus a fortress relief: at the waystation, a security company (30-55 tons) at Regular quality guarding a logistics node, with a supporting armor element and depot defenses, not built for a serious fight. The fortress's relief column is a heavier mobile reserve — a medium-to-heavy 'Mech force (50-80 tons), Regular-to-Veteran, detached to save the connector. The fortress itself is strong but fixed and bypassed; engaging it brings its full prepared weight.
opforSketch.behavior: Rear-area-depot doctrine: the waystation garrison defends a node it never expected to be the front, and holds for the relief rather than winning alone. The fortress reacts by detaching a relief to save its lifeline, racing to reach the depot before the seizure consolidates. The fortress proper stays put, a magnet for any attacker foolish enough to take it on instead of the connector behind it.

forks.name: OPERATION WITHERED VINE
forks.trigger: The waystation was seized and held; the fortress is cut off to wither and the advance moves on past it.
forks.consequence: The connector is taken and the fortress is an island, strong and useless, left to starve while the campaign rolls forward. {EMPLOYER} presses the advance from the captured node toward the next objective, the bypassed strongpoint forgotten behind the line. The leapfrog worked.

forks.name: OPERATION RECONNECTED
forks.trigger: The relief reopened the waystation, or the company was caught between the garrison and the column; the cut failed.
forks.consequence: The fortress kept its lifeline and the bypass did not take, and now the strongpoint's reserve is loose in the rear hunting the company that tried to strand it. The next operation is to hold the ground won and contain the situation while the campaign reconsiders — the fortress still connected, the easy cut spent. The plan bends; the strongpoint must be dealt with another way.

storyElementSeed: A depot quartermaster watching unfamiliar 'Mechs come over the rise from the wrong direction — the rear, the safe direction — and reaching for a radio to a fortress that suddenly cannot help.

merc.objectives.primary: Take the waystation behind the fortress and hold it long enough to cut the strongpoint's supply, then sit on it — the contract pays for the connector, not for a brawl with the fortress nobody asked you to storm.

RELIEF_DELAY_MIN.unit: minutes for the fortress relief to arrive

inspiration: A broad coalition of uneasy partners assaults a fanatical enemy's fortified homeworld, each contingent assigned its own sector, where the hardest part is that the enemy will not surrender and the allies barely trust each other.
skeleton: the player's company holds one coalition contingent's sector in the assault on a fanatical enemy's fortified homeworld, where the defender fights to the death and may scorch its own ground, the flanking sectors are held by uneasy allies whose pace the player cannot control, and the crux is taking a fortified zone whose neighbors may or may not keep abreast
title: OPERATION COMMON CAUSE
situation: Everyone who has a reason to want {TARGET_FACTION} gone has come to {WORLD} to finish it — a coalition of partners who agree on nothing else, landed in force to grind down the fanatics' fortified homeworld in {DISTRICT} sector by sector. Your company holds one sector of that line. The contingents on both flanks are allies you would not trust with your back in any other season. They advance on their own schedules toward their own objectives, and no order from above can fully guarantee they keep pace with you. {NPC:intel-source} reads your sector as held by a dug-in fanatic force, Veteran quality, fighting from prepared positions and rigged, like everything these people hold, to deny the ground rather than give it up. That picture is {INTEL_AGE_HOURS} hours old, and a defender who means to die in place fortifies to the end. The ground is hard and the company you keep makes it harder. The fortified sector — prepared urban and high positions — would be a stiff fight on its own, and your flanks are only as safe as allies you cannot command choose to make them. If the contingent beside you stalls, your flank opens; if it surges, your advance can lag behind. Push ahead of both and you form a salient the defender can pinch off. The enemy will not surrender. There is no breaking point to aim for and no morale to crack, only a fanatic garrison that fights to the last position and may burn its own sector at the end rather than let it be taken whole. The decision under the whole operation is how to advance through prepared ground while tied to neighbors whose pace you cannot set: match the coalition's tempo and stay aligned, or take your sector at your own speed and risk an open flank. {NPC:opfor-commander} commands your sector's defense and counts on the gaps between allies as much as on his own guns. Recommended force: {FORCE_SIZE}, the player's company in one coalition sector. Take your ground and keep your flanks, or surge alone into a salient and be cut off by an enemy who reads the gaps between allies.

objectives.primary: Clear and hold the assigned sector of the fortified homeworld assault, breaking the fanatic defense in your zone while keeping pace with the flanking contingents so the line advances together rather than in exposed salients.
objectives.secondary: Stop the defender from burning the sector's critical ground — the industry and infrastructure the coalition came to capture, not destroy — by reaching the demolition points before the fanatics can fire them.
objectives.bonus: Secure the boundary with at least one flanking contingent so neither ally's stall nor surge opens a gap. It proves the coalition can actually fight as one where it counts.

complications.name: Allies You Cannot Command
complications.text: The contingents on your flanks answer to their own commanders, their own politics, their own caution. One may push ahead for glory or its own objective; another may drag, husbanding its strength while you spend yours. You cannot order them, only react to them, and the defender knows it — the seams between uneasy allies are the softest part of any coalition line.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The flanking contingents advance on independent, partly unpredictable schedules; a flank may be secure, open, or overextended at any phase. The company's own pace interacts with theirs: surging ahead opens a flank the defender exploits, while matching a slow neighbor concedes time to the deepening defense.

complications.name: An Enemy That Will Not Yield
complications.text: These defenders will not break and will not surrender. There is no rout to trigger and no morale collapse to exploit, only a fanatic garrison that fights from each prepared position until it is destroyed. It treats every casualty it inflicts on you as a win. Pressure that would shatter an ordinary defense only buys ground here, meter by bloody meter.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The defense does not check morale and fights to destruction across the sector. Tactics that rely on breaking enemy will produce no collapse; the only way through is to take each position, and the longer it takes the more of the sector the fanatics expend in the taking.

complications.name: The Scorching
complications.text: A defender who will not yield ground may choose to ruin it instead. The fanatics may wire the sector's prize — the industry or infrastructure the coalition came to capture — to be destroyed at the end, denying it even in death. The fight is not only to take the ground but to reach the demolition points before they are fired and win a prize rather than a wasteland.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Demolition states may be active on the sector's critical ground; securing it intact requires reaching and disarming the charges under fire before the fanatics fire them. Failing voids the secondary objective and the coalition takes a ruin where it wanted a working asset.

complications.name: The Salient Trap
complications.text: Advance faster than your neighbors and you create a salient — a finger of your company pushed ahead of the line, flanks in the air, exactly the shape the defender wants. {NPC:opfor-commander} watches the coalition's pace and will turn on an overextended sector, pinching the salient off where the allies failed to keep abreast.
complications.mechanicalEffect: If the company advances significantly ahead of its flanking contingents, the defender concentrates against the resulting salient, threatening to cut it off; staying aligned with the slower neighbor avoids the trap but concedes tempo. The bonus (securing a seam) reduces this risk on that flank.

decisionPoints.name: Advancing the Sector
decisionPoints.context: Hard ground ahead, fanatics who will not quit, and allies whose pace you cannot set. You can match the coalition's tempo and stay aligned, push your own sector at speed and risk the salient, or spend effort securing a flank seam before driving on. Each answer trades the prize, your exposed flanks, and the coalition's cohesion differently.

options.title: Match the Coalition Tempo
advantages: Staying aligned with the flanking contingents keeps your flanks as secure as the line allows
Advancing together denies the defender the seams and salients he is counting on
disadvantages: Matching a slow neighbor concedes time to the deepening defense and the scorching clock
Your sector's pace is hostage to the most cautious ally on your flank
options.consequence: You keep the line whole and your flanks covered at the cost of tempo; the defense gets the time a slow advance gives it, but the fanatics get no salient to pinch and the prize is taken with secure flanks.

costs.resource: your sector's tempo tied to the slowest flanking contingent
costs.risk: A cautious neighbor's pace lets the defense deepen and the scorching clock run — the sector taken late, the prize perhaps already ruined

options.title: Take the Sector at Speed
advantages: A fast advance reaches the demolition points before the fanatics can scorch the prize
Speed takes the sector's ground while the defense is still setting, not after it has hardened
disadvantages: Outrunning your neighbors creates the salient the defender wants, flanks in the air
An overextended company can be pinched off where the allies failed to keep abreast
options.consequence: You go for the prize before it can be ruined and the ground before it hardens, at the risk of the salient; reach the charges in time and the sector is taken whole, but a defender who turns on your open flank may cut you off.

costs.resource: the company pushed ahead of the line, flanks exposed to the coalition's seams
costs.risk: A salient pinched off by the fanatics — cut off ahead of allies who did not keep up

options.title: Secure a Flank Seam First
advantages: Coordinating the boundary with a flanking contingent closes the seam the defender would exploit
A secured flank lets the company then advance at speed without the salient risk on that side
disadvantages: Spending effort on the seam — liaison, repositioning, waiting on an ally — costs time on the prize
The other flank remains uncertain, and the ally may not hold up its end of the boundary
options.consequence: You buy a secure flank by investing in the coalition seam, trading time for the cohesion that lets you then push hard; the boundary holds if the ally cooperates, but the effort concedes the defense time and covers only one side.

costs.resource: time and effort spent coordinating the flank seam rather than advancing on the prize
costs.risk: An uncooperative ally leaves the seam open despite the effort — time spent and the flank still soft

entries.event: The coalition assault opens; the company advances into its sector and the fanatic defense stands to in its prepared positions.
The flanking contingents' pace becomes apparent — one ahead, one behind, or both abreast; the defender begins reading the seams.
{NPC:opfor-commander} concentrates against the softest part of the line in his reach, and any scorching clock on the sector's prize begins.
The sector's critical ground is in reach if the advance held; the demolition points must be secured before the fanatics fire them.
The sector is cleared and held with its prize, or the fight congeals and the coalition line stalls; the assault's progress depends on every sector keeping up.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The assigned sector must be cleared, held, and its prize secured by T+24:00, in step with the coalition line. A sector that surges into a pinched-off salient, lags into a gap, or takes its ground only as a burned ruin fails the assault as surely as a sector overrun. Against an enemy who will not surrender, the only win is the ground taken whole with the line kept together.

opforSketch.composition: A fanatic homeworld defense: a dug-in force of mixed 'Mechs (35-90 tons) at Veteran quality fighting from prepared urban and high positions, supported by fixed emplacements and a street-fighting armor element, with combat engineers manning demolition states on the sector's critical ground. The defense fights to the last position and will scorch the prize rather than yield it. No reserve to break — only ground to take.
opforSketch.behavior: Fanatic last-ditch doctrine: hold every prepared position to destruction, scorch the prize rather than surrender it, and exploit the seams between uneasy coalition allies. The defense does not break or withdraw and imposes maximum cost; {NPC:opfor-commander} concentrates against salients and gaps in the coalition line, counting on the allies' mutual distrust to open the soft spot his own guns cannot.

forks.name: OPERATION KEPT FAITH
forks.trigger: The sector was taken whole and the line kept together; the coalition advances and the fanatics' homeworld is being reduced as one.
forks.consequence: Your sector is cleared, its prize intact, the flanks held — and the coalition, against the odds, is advancing as a line. {EMPLOYER}'s contingent presses to the next sector of the fortified zone, the uneasy alliance holding together one more bound. The common cause holds.

forks.name: OPERATION BROKEN LINE
forks.trigger: The sector stalled, was cut off in a salient, or fell only as a ruin; the coalition line broke step and the defense made it pay.
forks.consequence: The advance has lost its cohesion in your sector — a salient pinched off, a gap opened, a prize scorched — and the fanatics are exploiting the seam. The next operation is to hold the ground won and restore the flank while the coalition steadies its line, the assault checked and the allies blaming each other. The cause bends; the fanatics buy time on the coalition's distrust.

storyElementSeed: A liaison officer at a sector boundary trying to raise the allied contingent on a frequency that keeps not answering, while the advance waits and the demolition smoke starts to rise somewhere ahead.

comstar.objectives.primary: Clear and hold the assigned sector of the assault, breaking the heretic defense in your zone and keeping faith with the flanking contingents — the Order advances with strange company toward a shared and necessary end, and the line must hold as one where the work is done.

is-davion.objectives.primary: Clear and hold your sector of the assault, break the fanatic defense, and keep pace with the contingents on your flanks so the line advances together — the alliance is only as strong as its seams, and the enemy is hunting them.

FLANK_VARIANCE_MIN.unit: minutes of pace variance with the flanking contingents

inspiration: A raid is timed to a system-wide communications blackout, so that for a few precious hours the target cannot call for help and the relief that would normally come simply never learns there is anything to relieve.
skeleton: a company must hit a target during a window when the wider communications grid is down so the defender cannot summon relief, where the whole operation is shaped by the blackout's start and end rather than by distance to a relief force, and the danger is the grid coming back before the raid is clear and the call going out late
title: OPERATION SILENT HOUR
situation: The interstellar grid is down, and that silence is the whole operation. Since the wider communications net went dark, {WORLD} has been cut off: no fast word in or out of the system, every world thrown back on what it can reach by line of sight and local relay. {EMPLOYER} means to use the blackout. Hit the objective in {DISTRICT} during the hours the defender cannot call beyond the horizon for help, take what the raid came for, and be gone before the grid wakes and the call goes out. {NPC:intel-source} reads the objective as held by a standing garrison company, Regular quality, dug in around a target worth raiding — and, crucially, dependent on the off-world or cross-continent relief the blackout has cut off. That picture is {INTEL_AGE_HOURS} hours old, and a garrison that knows the grid is down may have grown jumpy. The terrain is ordinary; the clock is everything. The objective is a normal hard target — a garrisoned site to crack and loot or wreck — but the usual relief has been taken out of the equation. Normally the danger is how far the nearest reaction force sits and how fast it comes. Here there is no call for it to answer: for as long as the blackout holds, the garrison fights alone, and the raid's only real enemy is the moment the silence ends. The decision under the whole operation is timing against an uncertain window. No one knows exactly when the grid comes back — it could be hours yet, or any minute — and the raid is fast and clean only while the blackout holds. Hit early and you have margin but less time to prepare; cut it fine for a richer haul and you gamble the grid stays dark. {NPC:opfor-commander} commands the garrison and, cut off, will fight hard knowing no one is coming — until the silence breaks and suddenly someone might. Recommended force: {FORCE_SIZE}. Do the job inside the silent hours and vanish before the grid wakes, or still be on the objective when the blackout ends and the call for help finally crosses the horizon.

objectives.primary: Strike the objective and finish the raid's purpose — seizing its prize or destroying its function — within the communications blackout, then withdraw clear before the grid recovers and the garrison's call for relief can cross the horizon.
objectives.secondary: Disable the objective's local relay and line-of-sight links before striking, so that even during the blackout the garrison cannot raise the nearest cross-continent help by the means still working.
objectives.bonus: Recover the objective's record of the blackout's cause and expected length. It tells {EMPLOYER} how long the next silence might last and whether this one was an accident or someone's doing.

complications.name: The Uncertain Window
complications.text: Nobody knows when the grid comes back. The blackout has a start everyone felt and an end no one can predict — it could hold for hours yet or end in the next ten minutes. The raid is built on a clock whose length is a guess, and every minute spent on the objective is a minute closer to a silence that could break at any time.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Track the blackout as a window of uncertain length: a fixed safe minimum, after which each interval carries a growing chance the grid recovers. Once it does, the garrison can call for relief and the reaction equation switches back on. The raid must finish and clear before the recovery, with no certainty of how long it has.

complications.name: The Late Call
complications.text: When the grid wakes, the garrison's first act is to scream for help. If the raid is still on the objective, that call goes out with the raiders' description, strength, and heading attached. The blackout's whole value is silence, and the moment it ends with the company still in contact, that call chases the raid all the way home.
complications.mechanicalEffect: If the grid recovers while the company is still engaged or on the objective, the garrison transmits a full alert: a reaction force is summoned (its arrival a new clock) and the raid's withdrawal is now pursued and reported, raising the FAILURE fork's threat. Disabling the local relays first delays even this late call.

complications.name: The Isolated Garrison's Nerve
complications.text: A garrison that knows the grid is down knows it is alone, and an isolated defender fights differently — sometimes harder, with the desperation of no relief coming, sometimes more cautiously, husbanding itself because there is no replacing losses. {NPC:opfor-commander}'s posture under the blackout is its own unknown, and it shapes how the objective must be cracked.
complications.mechanicalEffect: On a roll at contact, the isolated garrison's posture is determined: it fights with extra tenacity (no relief, nothing to lose) or with extra caution (no relief, nothing to waste), changing whether the objective is best taken by overwhelming pressure or by maneuver around a defender unwilling to be drawn out.

complications.name: Local Eyes Still Work
complications.text: The interstellar grid is dark, but line of sight is not. Watchtowers, local relays, and a neighbor on the same continent can still pass a warning the short way, and the garrison may get a message out across the horizon even within the blackout if its local links are intact. The silence is only as complete as the raid makes it.
complications.mechanicalEffect: If the objective's local relay and line-of-sight links are not disabled first, the garrison can summon nearby cross-continent help even during the blackout (a shorter, lesser reaction than the full grid call, but real); disabling them first preserves the full value of the silence.

decisionPoints.name: Timing the Silence
decisionPoints.context: An uncertain window, a hard target, and a clock no one can read. You can hit early for the safety margin, cut it fine for a richer and more thorough job, or spend the opening minutes killing the local links to deepen the silence first. Each answer trades the margin against the blackout, the completeness of the raid, and the risk of the late call.

options.title: Hit Early, Keep Margin
advantages: Striking as soon as possible banks the most blackout time against the uncertain recovery
The widest cushion to finish and withdraw before the grid can wake
disadvantages: Less time to prepare the strike means a rougher, possibly less complete job
An early hit may forgo the richer haul or the relay-disabling that a setup would allow
options.consequence: You buy safety with speed, going in before you are fully set to be sure of beating the grid; the raid is clean and clear with margin to spare, but rougher and perhaps less thorough than a prepared strike.

costs.resource: preparation and completeness traded for the widest margin against the grid's recovery
costs.risk: A rushed early strike achieves less than the objective offered — clear in time, but the haul thin

options.title: Cut It Fine for the Full Haul
advantages: More time to prepare and execute means a thorough job — the full prize, the relays down, the records taken
A complete raid extracts everything the objective is worth
disadvantages: Every extra minute gambles that the blackout holds, with no way to know when it ends
A grid that wakes mid-raid catches the company on the objective with the late call going out
options.consequence: You go for everything the silence can give, staking the clean getaway on the blackout lasting; do it and the raid is total, but cut it too fine and the grid wakes with you still in contact and the call goes out.

costs.resource: the safety margin spent on a thorough, complete raid
costs.risk: The grid recovers mid-raid — caught on the objective with a full alert broadcasting the company's description and heading

options.title: Kill the Local Links First
advantages: Disabling the relays and line-of-sight links deepens the silence, denying even the local cross-continent call
Buys insurance against the late call — a grid that wakes finds the objective unable to transmit at once
disadvantages: Spending the opening minutes on the links delays the strike itself, eating the blackout margin
The relays may be guarded or dispersed — disabling them is a small operation of its own
options.consequence: You make the silence as total as it can be before striking, trading time for a deeper blackout; the garrison stays truly cut off, but the minutes spent on the links are minutes the uncertain window is counting down.

costs.resource: time and effort spent disabling the local links before the main strike
costs.risk: Time on the relays lets the uncertain window close before the objective is even hit — the silence deepened but the raid late

entries.event: The company strikes the objective within the blackout; the garrison stands to and finds, as expected, that it cannot raise help beyond the horizon.
{NPC:opfor-commander} fights the raid as an isolated garrison, its posture — tenacious or cautious — becoming clear.
The raid's purpose should be achieved by now; the blackout has passed its safe minimum and every minute risks the grid waking.
The company should be withdrawing and clear of the objective; the chance of the grid recovering climbs with each interval.
If the grid wakes with the company still in contact, the garrison's call crosses the horizon and a reaction force is summoned to a raid no longer silent.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The raid must be done and the company clear before the communications grid recovers — an uncertain moment that grows likelier after the safe minimum and is assumed to arrive by T+22:00. A company still on the objective when the silence breaks has its call-for-help, its description, and its heading broadcast at once, and the raid that depended on silence is then hunted by a reaction force that knows everything.

opforSketch.composition: An isolated garrison: a standing garrison company of mixed 'Mechs (35-65 tons) at Regular quality, dug in around the objective, supported by an armor element and fixed defenses, reliant on relief that the blackout has cut off. If the grid recovers in time, a summoned reaction force — a fresh medium lance or company — arrives to pursue. The garrison's posture under isolation (tenacious or cautious) varies.
opforSketch.behavior: Isolated-garrison doctrine under a comms blackout: the garrison defends knowing no help is coming, fighting either with the desperation of no relief or the caution of no replacements, and tries to get a warning out by any local link still working. The whole defense is shaped by the silence; the moment the grid wakes, it screams for help and any summoned reaction force hunts the withdrawing raid with full information.

forks.name: OPERATION KEPT QUIET
forks.trigger: The raid was done and the company clear before the grid woke; no call ever crossed the horizon.
forks.consequence: The job is finished and, as far as anyone beyond {WORLD} knows, nothing happened — the silence held and the raid never made the net. {EMPLOYER} exploits the unbroken secrecy with a follow-on while the defender is still piecing together what hit it, the recovered blackout intelligence hinting at when the next silence might fall.

forks.name: OPERATION LATE WORD
forks.trigger: The grid woke with the company still in contact, or the local links carried a call; the alert went out with the raid's description attached.
forks.consequence: The silence broke too soon and the call for help crossed the horizon, the raiders' strength and heading with it. The next operation is to break clear and off {WORLD} ahead of a reaction force now hunting a known quantity — the raid that depended on silence undone by the late word. The plan bends; the silence failed.

storyElementSeed: A garrison radio operator keying a dead channel out of habit, getting nothing but the hiss of a grid that has been down for hours, while the firing starts somewhere on the perimeter and the help that channel used to reach is still a silence.

is-davion.objectives.primary: Strike the objective and finish the job inside the communications blackout, then be clear before the grid recovers and the garrison can call for relief — the silence is the whole plan, so do the work and be gone before it ends.

inspiration: A counter-battery hunt where the enemy's guns fire from concealment and shift between salvos, so the entire problem is finding where they are before they can be silenced — the locating, not the killing, is the mission.
skeleton: a recon-strike company must locate an enemy's concealed, displacing fire support that is punishing friendly movement from hidden positions, where finding the guns by their signatures before they shift is the whole problem, the kill is trivial once located, and every probe to flush them risks becoming the target
title: OPERATION SOUNDING LINE
situation: Something on {WORLD} is killing {EMPLOYER}'s movement in {DISTRICT}, and no one can find it. {TARGET_FACTION} has placed fire support — long-range guns and missile batteries — in the broken high ground, and they are punishing every friendly advance from positions no one can fix. They fire a salvo and shift to a new hide before the counter-fire can fall. The advance has stalled, not because the enemy line is strong, but because crossing the open ground under that unseen fire is bleeding the force white. Your company is sent to do the one thing that breaks the problem: find the guns. {NPC:intel-source} reads the enemy fire support as a reinforced battery group, Regular-to-Veteran quality, screened by a light covering force and expert at hiding and moving. That picture is {INTEL_AGE_HOURS} hours old, and a battery that lives by moving has moved since. The high ground is the whole problem. It is a maze of ridge, draw, and cover — jungle-choked or rock-broken depending on the slope — that hides a gun a hundred meters off the track and swallows the flash and smoke that would give it away. The guns are heard and felt but never seen. Killing one is easy once you know where it is: a located battery is a dead battery. The hard part is the locating, and it comes with a cruel catch. The surest way to find a hidden gun is to give it a target worth shooting at, which means whatever flushes the battery is standing in its sights. Every probe to make the guns reveal themselves risks the prober becoming the next salvo's mark. {NPC:opfor-commander} commands the fire support and will keep moving, trading ground for the concealment that keeps his guns alive and his fire falling. Recommended force: {FORCE_SIZE}, recon-strike — eyes that can also kill what they find. Locate the batteries and silence them so the advance can move, or grope through the high ground feeding the guns targets until the force gives up the ground.

objectives.primary: Locate the enemy's hidden fire-support positions before they can move out of reach, and destroy enough of them to free friendly movement across the contested ground, breaking the unseen fire that has stalled the advance.
objectives.secondary: Map the battery group's movement pattern — the routes and hide sites it cycles between — so the positions you cannot reach this time can be predicted and struck later.
objectives.bonus: Capture the group's fire-control element intact. Losing it blinds the surviving guns, and its records reveal the whole indirect-fire plan for the sector.

complications.name: Find It to Kill It
complications.text: The kill is the easy part. A gun whose position is known dies to a single accurate strike; there is no hard fight in destroying a located battery. The whole mission turns on finding them. The guns are hidden in ground built to hide them, and until one is fixed it cannot be touched, only endured. Every minute you spend not finding them is a minute the advance bleeds.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Enemy fire-support positions are hidden and must be located — through their signatures, by observation, or by drawing fire — before they can be engaged. Once a position is fixed, destroying it is straightforward. The operation is scored on positions located and silenced, not on a stand-up fight.

complications.name: The Displacing Guns
complications.text: The batteries do not wait to be found. They fire and move — a salvo, then a shift to the next hide before the counter can fall — so a position fixed one minute is empty the next. Locating a gun is only useful if it is struck before it displaces, and a company that finds the battery a moment too late finds only the warm, abandoned ground it fired from.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Located positions are perishable: a fixed battery displaces after a set interval unless struck first. The company must convert each location into a strike quickly, and mapping the displacement pattern (the secondary) lets it intercept guns at their next position rather than chase empty hides.

complications.name: The Bait Is the Prober
complications.text: The fastest way to find a hidden gun is to show it something it cannot resist shooting. But whatever flushes the battery is standing in its sights. To draw the fire that reveals a position, you have to take that fire. Every deliberate attempt to make the guns show themselves puts the prober under the very salvo that gives the position away.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Drawing fire to locate a battery exposes the baiting element to that fire: locating by provocation carries a real chance of casualties to the prober. A commander trades the speed of flushing the guns against the cost of being the bait that does it.

complications.name: The Covering Screen
complications.text: The guns do not sit unguarded. A light covering force screens the battery positions and the displacement routes, there to fend off exactly the kind of recon-strike sent to hunt them — to delay the locators, give warning, and buy the guns time to shift. The screen is not the objective, but it stands between the company and every position it needs to fix.
complications.mechanicalEffect: A light covering force contests the company's reconnaissance, screening the battery positions and slowing the locating effort; it fights to delay and warn rather than to win, trading itself for the guns' time to displace. Brushing it aside costs time the displacing batteries use.

decisionPoints.name: Hunting the Guns
decisionPoints.context: Hidden, shifting guns and a force bleeding under them. You can sweep methodically to fix positions by observation, deliberately bait the batteries into firing to flush them fast, or push for the fire-control node to blind the whole group at once. Each answer trades the speed of finding the guns against the cost of being shot at and the completeness of the silencing.

options.title: Sweep and Observe
advantages: Methodical reconnaissance fixes positions by their signatures without deliberately drawing fire
Builds the displacement map (the secondary) as it goes, enabling future strikes on hides out of reach now
disadvantages: A careful sweep is slow, and slow lets the batteries keep firing on the stalled advance
Positions found by patient observation may displace before the strike can reach them
options.consequence: You find the guns the safe way, taking few casualties to the search itself but conceding time; the advance keeps bleeding while you work, and some batteries shift before you can convert a location to a kill.

costs.resource: time spent on a methodical sweep while the advance bleeds under the unseen fire
costs.risk: The slow search lets batteries displace before they can be struck — guns located too late, ground still denied

options.title: Bait the Batteries
advantages: Deliberately drawing fire flushes the hidden guns fast — the quickest way to fix positions and free the advance
A battery that fires on the bait reveals itself for an immediate strike before it can displace
disadvantages: The baiting element is the target — flushing the guns means taking their fire to do it
Repeated baiting bleeds the prober, and a battery may shift between the bait and the strike anyway
options.consequence: You trade blood for speed, offering the guns a target to make them show themselves; the positions fall fast if the strike follows quickly, but the company pays for each location in the fire it drew to find it.

costs.resource: the baiting element exposed to the very fire that locates the guns
costs.risk: Casualties to the bait mount as the batteries are flushed — the guns found at the price of the force that found them

options.title: Hunt the Fire-Control Node
advantages: Taking or destroying the coordination node blinds the surviving guns and reveals the whole fire plan
One decisive strike on the node can break the battery group's coordination across the sector at a stroke
disadvantages: The fire-control element is the best-hidden and best-guarded part of the group — finding it is the hardest search of all
Committing to the node means passing up the guns you could have located in the meantime
options.consequence: You go for the brain instead of the limbs, betting that blinding the coordination unhinges the whole group; find the node and the guns fall silent together, but the search for it is the longest gamble and the advance bleeds while you hunt.

costs.resource: the search concentrated on the elusive fire-control node rather than the individual guns
costs.risk: A long, fruitless hunt for the node leaves the guns un-located and firing — the gamble lost, the advance still stalled

entries.event: The company enters the high ground; the enemy batteries continue firing on the stalled advance from concealment and the covering screen contests the recon.
First positions are located by observation or by drawn fire; {NPC:opfor-commander} begins displacing the revealed guns to fresh hides.
The displacement pattern starts to emerge; located batteries must be struck before they shift or chased to their next positions.
Enough of the fire support is silenced or mapped to begin freeing friendly movement, or the guns are still shifting faster than they can be fixed.
The unseen fire is broken and the advance can move, or the batteries have kept displacing and the force must reckon with ground it still cannot cross.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: Enough of the enemy fire support must be located and silenced by T+24:00 to free friendly movement across the contested ground. Batteries that keep moving faster than they can be fixed leave the advance bleeding under fire it still cannot see, and a hunt that finds only warm, empty hides has spent the company for ground that stays denied.

opforSketch.composition: Concealed, displacing fire support plus a light screen: a reinforced battery group of long-range 'Mechs and combat vehicles (fire-support behavior, LRM and long-range weapons) at Regular-to-Veteran quality, expert at concealment and displacement, coordinated by a hidden fire-control element. A light covering force (fast light 'Mechs and vehicles) screens the positions and routes. The guns are deadly at range and fragile once found; the screen fights to delay.
opforSketch.behavior: Shoot-and-scoot fire-support doctrine: fire a salvo, displace before the counter falls, and never hold a position long enough to be fixed. The covering screen delays and warns the recon-strike force to buy the guns time to shift; the fire-control node stays hidden and coordinates the displacement. The whole group trades ground for the concealment that keeps it alive, betting it can keep killing the advance from hides faster than it can be hunted down.

forks.name: OPERATION CLEAR RANGE
forks.trigger: Enough of the fire support was located and silenced to free the advance; the unseen guns are unseen no longer.
forks.consequence: The batteries are broken or mapped and friendly movement is free across the ground they denied, the displacement pattern in hand for any guns that fled. {EMPLOYER} resumes the stalled advance now that the killing fire is silenced, your company exploiting the ground it just opened. The hunt paid.

forks.name: OPERATION STILL BLIND
forks.trigger: The batteries kept displacing faster than they could be fixed; the unseen fire still owns the contested ground.
forks.consequence: The guns slipped the hunt and the advance is still bleeding under fire no one can see, the company itself now worn from the search. The next operation is to hold the line and protect friendly movement as best it can while the fire-support problem is reckoned with another way — the ground still denied, the guns still hidden. The hunt bends; the batteries keep firing.

storyElementSeed: A scout 'Mech holding stock-still in a draw, the pilot watching a ridgeline for the flash that means a gun and knowing that the moment to see it is also the moment it sees back.

is-davion.objectives.primary: Find the enemy's hidden guns before they can shift and kill enough of them to get the advance moving again — the locating is the whole job, so fix the batteries and silence them before they bleed the force off the ground.

merc.objectives.primary: Locate the concealed fire support and silence enough of it to free movement across the contested ground. The contract pays for the guns found and killed; warm empty hides and a bled company are the worst invoice there is.

DISPLACE_INTERVAL_MIN.unit: minutes before a fixed battery displaces

inspiration: A decoy convoy that looks like easy prey is rigged to bait commerce-raiders into committing, then turns out to be an armed trap that springs once the raiders are too close to run.
skeleton: a hunter must disguise its strength as a soft merchant convoy to lure scarcity-driven raiders into committing to an attack, then spring the trap once they are too close to flee, where the whole problem is selling the bait convincingly enough to draw a cautious predator and timing the reveal so the raiders cannot escape the ambush
title: OPERATION FALSE CARGO
situation: Raiders have been bleeding the supply runs across {DISTRICT} on {WORLD}, and they have gotten good at it. They hit the soft convoys, fade before any escort can close, and never commit to a fight they might lose. {EMPLOYER} has stopped chasing them and set a trap instead. The plan is a convoy rigged to look like exactly the soft prey the raiders have been feeding on — slow, lightly escorted, hauling cargo worth the risk — that is in truth your company in disguise, waiting to spring once the raiders commit too close to run. {NPC:intel-source} reads the raider band as a scarcity-driven outfit of mixed light 'Mechs and fast vehicles, Regular quality at best but cunning, that strikes only when the odds look certain and breaks contact the instant they do not. That picture is {INTEL_AGE_DAYS} days old, and a raider's strength shifts with whatever it has lately stolen. The ground is chosen for the trap. The convoy route runs through open frontier where a raider can watch a column from far off, and, crucially, it passes one stretch — a defile, a dry crossing, a coastal narrows — where a committed attacker cannot easily break off. Selling the bait is the whole problem. The raiders are cautious and will not commit to a convoy that looks wrong, so the disguise means a column that genuinely looks vulnerable, which means accepting real exposure to draw a real attacker. Then comes the timing. Spring too early and the raiders fade as they always do; spring too late and the disguised escort takes real losses playing the victim. {NPC:opfor-commander} leads the band and has survived this long by trusting nothing. The lure has to be good enough to beat his caution, and the reveal sharp enough to shut the trap before he bolts. Recommended force: {FORCE_SIZE}, hidden inside a convoy's skin. Sell the bait and spring it clean, or show your teeth too soon and watch a careful raider slip the hook one more time.

objectives.primary: Lure the raider band into committing to an attack on the disguised convoy, then spring the trap once they are too close to break off, destroying or capturing enough of the band to end the raids on {EMPLOYER}'s supply runs.
objectives.secondary: Keep the convoy disguise convincing enough that the band commits fully rather than just probing. Sell real vulnerability without taking crippling losses before the reveal.
objectives.bonus: Take the raider leadership alive — {NPC:opfor-commander} and the band's navigator. What they know about the raiders' base, their fences, and the other soft routes turns one ambush into the unraveling of the whole operation.

complications.name: Selling the Bait
complications.text: A cautious predator does not bite a trap that smells of one. The convoy has to look genuinely soft — real cargo, a thin and plausible escort, the unguarded moments a raider watches for — because a band that has survived by trusting nothing will fade from anything that seems too easy or too odd. Selling the disguise means accepting real exposure; a column that is obviously a trap catches nothing.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The convoy's disguise is tracked against the raiders' caution. Holding too much strength visibly, or springing prematurely, reads as a trap and the band probes or withdraws instead of committing; selling genuine vulnerability (accepting some exposure of the decoy elements) is required to draw a full commitment.

complications.name: Timing the Reveal
complications.text: The trap works only in a narrow window. Spring it early, while the raiders can still turn and run, and the cautious band fades as it always does, the ambush wasted. Spring it late, after the disguised escort has played victim through real attacks, and the decoy elements take genuine losses before they can fight back. The reveal has to fall in the moment the raiders are committed but not yet winning.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Track the raiders' commitment: the trap should spring once they are past the disengagement point but before the decoy takes crippling damage. An early reveal lets the band escape (failing the primary); a late one inflicts real losses on the disguised force before the ambush turns.

complications.name: The Disengagement Ground
complications.text: The whole route is chosen so that, at one stretch, a committed attacker cannot easily break off — a defile, a crossing, a narrows past which the raiders are caught. Drawing the band onto that ground before the reveal is the art of it; raiders that commit before the trap-ground, or hang back from it, can still run when the teeth come out.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The ambush's effectiveness depends on the raiders being on the disengagement-limiting terrain when the trap springs. Springing while they are still on open, escapable ground lets the faster raiders flee; luring them onto the chosen ground first seals the trap.

complications.name: A Predator Who Trusts Nothing
complications.text: {NPC:opfor-commander} has survived a long time by assuming every easy meal is a trap. He may probe with a fraction of his strength first, may hold his best units back, may break off at the first wrong note and not be tempted again. The band's caution is the real adversary — not its guns, which are beatable once committed, but its unwillingness to commit at all.
complications.mechanicalEffect: On a roll at the raiders' approach, the band probes cautiously rather than committing fully, testing the convoy with an expendable element; only a convincing performance against the probe draws the full band in, while a botched response or a premature reveal confirms the predator's suspicion and he withdraws his main strength.

decisionPoints.name: Setting the Hook
decisionPoints.context: A cautious predator, a disguised column, and one stretch of ground where a committed raider cannot run. You can play it soft and patient to draw a full commitment, dangle an irresistible prize to overcome the band's caution, or spring early and sure to bag whatever has committed so far. Each answer trades the size of the catch against the risk of the band slipping the hook.

options.title: Play It Soft and Patient
advantages: A convincingly vulnerable convoy drawn deep onto the trap-ground lures the full band into committing
Patience bags the whole outfit, leadership included, rather than a fraction
disadvantages: Playing victim longer means the decoy elements absorb real attacks before the reveal
The longer the bait runs, the more chances the cautious raider has to sense the trap and fade
options.consequence: You go for the whole band by selling the bait all the way onto the killing ground, at the cost of real punishment to the decoy first; spring it right and the outfit is finished, but every extra minute as the victim is risk and damage taken.

costs.resource: the decoy elements exposed to real raider attacks while the bait is sold all the way in
costs.risk: The band senses the trap during the long bait and fades — punishment taken for a catch that slips away

options.title: Dangle an Irresistible Prize
advantages: A cargo too rich to pass up can overcome even a cautious predator's suspicion and draw a full commitment fast
Greed shortens the patient game — the band commits sooner, less time for the decoy to take losses
disadvantages: A prize valuable enough to be irresistible is a prize you genuinely risk if the trap fails
An obviously rich convoy that is too lightly guarded may read as a trap to a truly careful raider
options.consequence: You bet on greed beating caution, putting up real bait to draw a fast full commitment; the band bites hard if the prize sells, but a failed trap means the valuable lure is genuinely lost to the raiders.

costs.resource: a genuinely valuable cargo risked as the lure to overcome the raiders' caution
costs.risk: The trap fails and the rich bait is actually taken — the hook lost and the prize with it

options.title: Spring Early and Sure
advantages: Revealing as soon as part of the band commits bags whatever has taken the bait with the least risk to the decoy
A sure, early spring avoids the chance of the whole performance being read as a trap
disadvantages: An early reveal catches only the committed fraction; the cautious main body and the leadership escape
A band that loses a probe and keeps its strength simply stops taking the bait and moves on to softer routes
options.consequence: You take the safe, smaller catch, springing before the band is fully in to be sure of something; the committed element is destroyed, but the careful core slips away to raid another run, the operation a partial win at best.

costs.resource: the full catch traded for a sure, early spring on whatever has committed
costs.risk: Only the probe is bagged — the main band and the leadership escape to raid elsewhere, the problem unsolved

entries.event: The disguised convoy moves along the chosen route; the raider band, watching, begins to size it up as prey.
The band tests the convoy — a probe or a cautious approach; the disguise must hold to draw it in further.
If the bait sells, the raiders commit and close onto the disengagement-limiting ground; the reveal window approaches.
The trap springs — the convoy shows its teeth once the raiders are past the point of easy escape, or the moment is missed and the band reacts.
The band is destroyed or taken in the ambush, or the cautious core has broken contact and slipped away to softer routes.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: The trap must be sprung while the raiders are committed onto the disengagement-limiting ground but before the decoy is crippled, by roughly T+15:00. Spring too early and the cautious band fades as it always has; spring too late and the disguised force is mauled playing the victim. And a band that slips the hook learns the convoys are baited and never bites again.

opforSketch.composition: A scarcity-driven raider band: mixed light 'Mechs (20-40 tons) and fast combat vehicles (hover and wheeled, hit-and-run behavior) at Green-to-Regular quality, cunning and cautious, built for ambushing soft targets and fleeing hard ones. The band may probe with an expendable element before committing its main strength and leadership. Beatable once committed; the whole challenge is making it commit and sealing its escape.
opforSketch.behavior: Opportunist-raider doctrine: strike only when the odds look certain, break contact the instant they sour, and never commit to a stand-up fight. The band probes suspicious prey, holds its best back, and trusts nothing — its caution is its survival. Once genuinely committed onto bad ground it fights to escape rather than to win, making the timing of the trap, not its firepower, the decisive factor.

forks.name: OPERATION FULL NET
forks.trigger: The band committed and the trap sprung clean; the raiders are destroyed or taken and the raids are ended.
forks.consequence: The outfit that bled the supply runs is finished, and if the leadership was taken, it has given up the base and the other soft routes. {EMPLOYER} moves on the raiders' lair while the band is broken and leaderless — turning one clean ambush into the end of the whole nest. The fishing paid.

forks.name: OPERATION SLIPPED HOOK
forks.trigger: The reveal came wrong or the band sensed the trap; the cautious core slipped away and now knows the convoys are baited.
forks.consequence: The hook missed and the raiders got away wiser, and a band that knows the convoys are traps will not be fooled again — it will hit harder and warier from here. The next operation is to hunt the band the hard way, on its own ground, now that the easy fishing is spent. The trap bends; the predator learned.
